verses.text: When it was determined that we should sail for Italy, they delivered Paul and certain other prisoners to a centurion named Julius, of the Augustan band.
Embarking in a ship of Adramyttium, which was about to sail to places on the coast of Asia, we put to sea; Aristarchus, a Macedonian of Thessalonica, being with us.
The next day, we touched at Sidon. Julius treated Paul kindly, and gave him permission to go to his friends and refresh himself.
Putting to sea from there, we sailed under the lee of Cyprus, because the winds were contrary.
When we had sailed across the sea which is off Cilicia and Pamphylia, we came to Myra, a city of Lycia.
There the centurion found a ship of Alexandria sailing for Italy, and he put us on board.
When we had sailed slowly many days, and had come with difficulty opposite Cnidus, the wind not allowing us further, we sailed under the lee of Crete, opposite Salmone.
With difficulty sailing along it we came to a certain place called Fair Havens, near the city of Lasea.
When much time had passed and the voyage was now dangerous, because the Fast had now already gone by, Paul admonished them,
and said to them, “Sirs, I perceive that the voyage will be with injury and much loss, not only of the cargo and the ship, but also of our lives.”
But the centurion gave more heed to the master and to the owner of the ship than to those things which were spoken by Paul.

Because the haven was not suitable to winter in, the majority advised going to sea from there, if by any means they could reach Phoenix, and winter there, which is a port of Crete, looking northeast and southeast.
When the south wind blew softly, supposing that they had obtained their purpose, they weighed anchor and sailed along Crete, close to shore.
But before long, a stormy wind beat down from shore, which is called Euroclydon.
When the ship was caught, and couldn’t face the wind, we gave way to it, and were driven along.
Running under the lee of a small island called Clauda, we were able, with difficulty, to secure the boat.
After they had hoisted it up, they used cables to help reinforce the ship. Fearing that they would run aground on the Syrtis sand bars, they lowered the sea anchor, and so were driven along.
As we labored exceedingly with the storm, the next day they began to throw things overboard.
On the third day, they threw out the ship’s tackle with their own hands.
When neither sun nor stars shone on us for many days, and no small storm pressed on us, all hope that we would be saved was now taken away.
When they had been long without food, Paul stood up in the middle of them, and said, “Sirs, you should have listened to me, and not have set sail from Crete, and have gotten this injury and loss.
Now I exhort you to cheer up, for there will be no loss of life among you, but only of the ship.
For there stood by me this night an angel, belonging to the God whose I am and whom I serve,
saying, ‘Don’t be afraid, Paul. You must stand before Caesar. Behold, God has granted you all those who sail with you.’
Therefore, sirs, cheer up! For I believe God, that it will be just as it has been spoken to me.
But we must run aground on a certain island.”
But when the fourteenth night had come, as we were driven back and forth in the Adriatic Sea, about midnight the sailors surmised that they were drawing near to some land.
They took soundings, and found twenty fathoms.  After a little while, they took soundings again, and found fifteen fathoms.
Fearing that we would run aground on rocky ground, they let go four anchors from the stern, and wished for daylight.
As the sailors were trying to flee out of the ship, and had lowered the boat into the sea, pretending that they would lay out anchors from the bow,
Paul said to the centurion and to the soldiers, “Unless these stay in the ship, you can’t be saved.”
Then the soldiers cut away the ropes of the boat, and let it fall off.
While the day was coming on, Paul begged them all to take some food, saying, “Today is the fourteenth day that you wait and continue fasting, having taken nothing.
Therefore I beg you to take some food, for this is for your safety; for not a hair will perish from any of your heads.”
When he had said this, and had taken bread, he gave thanks to God in the presence of all, and he broke it, and began to eat.
Then they all cheered up, and they also took food.
In all, we were two hundred seventy-six souls on the ship.
When they had eaten enough, they lightened the ship, throwing out the wheat into the sea.
When it was day, they didn’t recognize the land, but they noticed a certain bay with a beach, and they decided to try to drive the ship onto it.
Casting off the anchors, they left them in the sea, at the same time untying the rudder ropes. Hoisting up the foresail to the wind, they made for the beach.
But coming to a place where two seas met, they ran the vessel aground. The bow struck and remained immovable, but the stern began to break up by the violence of the waves.
The soldiers’ counsel was to kill the prisoners, so that none of them would swim out and escape.
But the centurion, desiring to save Paul, stopped them from their purpose, and commanded that those who could swim should throw themselves overboard first to go toward the land;
and the rest should follow, some on planks, and some on other things from the ship. So they all escaped safely to the land.

footnotes.content: A soldier's job was to deliver prisoners—no questions asked. Yet notice how quickly God arranges that Paul, a man in chains, travels under Julius's watch. Even authority, even pagan Rome, serves the Lord's purpose without knowing it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Aristarchus, from Thessalonica, travels with Paul as a companion—not because he had to, but because friendship draws you into the master's path. What a gift, to stay close when the road gets hard.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Sidon was a known port stop on the coast. Julius shows gentleness here—Paul, though a prisoner, goes ashore to strengthen himself with friends. This small mercy plants no seed yet, but mercy never returns empty.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The winds were contrary, so they sheltered under Cyprus's lee. We sail knowing the wind will resist us—that's no surprise to the Lord. Even contrary winds are part of His route.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Myra was the main port for Egypt's grain ships. The journey unfolds on schedule—Cilicia, Pamphylia, then Myra. Sometimes the mundane stages of travel are just that: stages on the way to where He's leading.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: An Alexandrian ship bound for Italy—exactly what they need. Do you see the quiet providence? The right ship arrives at the right moment. The Lord doesn't shout; He simply has things in place.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Cnidus sits where the Aegean meets the Mediterranean—the winds fought them hard there. Progress was slow and difficult. Yet every slow day still moved them forward. Patience is its own kind of faith.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Fair Havens, near Lasea in Crete, was a poor shelter for winter. The name's irony would not escape the sailors as the storm began to brew. A place called 'safe' can harbor the deepest test.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Paul speaks up now—not to show off his wisdom, but to warn those in his care. The Fast (Yom Kippur, in autumn) marks the season when sailing grew perilous. He reads the signs and speaks truth, even to strangers.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A prisoner prophesies danger—loss of cargo, ship, and lives. His words are exact and weightily spoken. Yet no one believes him. How often do we refuse wisdom because it comes from an unexpected voice?
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The centurion trusts the ship's master and owner—they were experts, after all. But expertise alone cannot see what the Spirit whispers. Sometimes the loudest voices drown out the still, small warning.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The majority voted to sail onward to Phoenix, a better harbor. Democracy is not evil, but neither is it infallible. The crowd's wish became the ship's course—a choice they would soon regret.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A soft south wind seems to grant their wish. Oh, how we mistake ease for approval! One gentle breeze and all doubt dissolves. But the Lord sometimes lets us sail into the storm to teach us trust.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Euroclydon—a northeast storm wind—swept down from the mountains of Crete. Sailors knew this wind's name and its fury. What came soft became fierce, and they had no shelter left to find.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The ship couldn't face the wind, so it gave way. They surrendered to the storm's push. Sometimes we, too, must stop fighting and let the Lord carry us where He will.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Clauda was a small island—they gripped its shelter just long enough to secure the lifeboat. Every small mercy in a storm is a whisper of God's hand. We are never beyond His reach.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They used cables to wrap and brace the hull—a last-ditch effort called 'frapping.' Then they dropped the sea anchor to drift. All their strength and all their hope rested on improvisation and prayer.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Day after day they threw cargo overboard to lighten the load. Each thing tossed away was a loss, but keeping the ship mattered more. Sometimes we must let go of what we've held dear.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: By the third day, they threw out the ship's tackle with their own hands—the very equipment that might save them. Desperation strips away prudence. At that depth of fear, they were throwing away their tools of escape.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: No sun, no stars, no way to navigate. The darkness was complete—fourteen days of it. Yet here is where faith begins: when all your charts fail and you can't see an inch ahead.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Paul stands up, having fasted fourteen days like everyone else. His words are blunt: 'You should have listened.' But he doesn't scold from safety—he's suffered the same hunger, the same terror.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: After fourteen days of despair, Paul's command pierces through: 'Cheer up.' Not false comfort, but the voice of someone who knows the Lord is at work. The ship will be lost, but you will be saved. Only faith could speak that sentence.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: An angel stood beside Paul in the night—not visible to the crowd, but real. 'The God whose I am and whom I serve.' Even in the pit of the sea, Paul's allegiance remains steady. Ownership and service: that's the anchor.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: 'You must stand before Caesar'—the journey's end is set. And those who sail with you will be saved by his presence. Paul's calling is their safety. Grace doesn't save him alone; it spreads to all aboard.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: 'I believe God, that it will be just as it has been spoken to me.' In the dark, with food gone and hope shipwrecked, Paul rests on one thing: the word spoken in the night. That is all faith ever needs.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: An island waits ahead. Not Rome, not safety as they'd planned, but an island. The Lord's mercy comes different than we expect, yet it comes. We must run aground—we must let go of the ship to be saved.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The fourteenth night—land was near. Sailors, trained to read the sea's signs, felt it in their bones. After fourteen days, the deliverance was at hand, though no one yet could see the shore.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Sounding line and fathom—twenty, then fifteen. These nautical measurements were the sailor's language of depth and hope. Closer, closer. The bottom rose toward them like an answer to prayer.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Four anchors from the stern. Once they felt bottom approaching, the crew's fear sharpened—rocky ground might tear the hull to pieces. They dropped all their anchors at once and prayed for daylight.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The sailors attempt to slip away in the lifeboat, pretending to lay out anchors from the bow—a lie born of cowardice. In crisis, the mask slips. Men abandon the post when fear grabs hard enough.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Paul's voice cuts through the darkness: 'Unless these stay in the ship, you can't be saved.' A prisoner gives orders. The centurion listens. Something in Paul's certainty commands obedience—the Spirit's authority flows through him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The soldiers cut the ropes and let the boat fall away. It was the right act, though it looked harsh. Sometimes trust means severing what seems like escape, because the real rescue lies in staying bound to the ship's crew.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Paul begs them all to eat—after fourteen days without food. His concern is practical, not sentimental. A starving crew won't have the strength to survive the wreck. Love feeds the hungry before heroics.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: 'Not a hair will perish from any of your heads.' Again Paul speaks the angel's promise aloud—all will be saved. This is not sentimentality; it's truth spoken as weapon against despair.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Paul takes bread, gives thanks to God before all of them, and eats. In the hold of a dying ship, he practices gratitude. This is the grandest act of faith: giving thanks when the outcome is still unknown.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Suddenly they all cheered up and ate. One man's confidence, one man's prayer—it spread like light through the hold. Faith is contagious when it comes from someone who walks it out.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Two hundred seventy-six souls—the count matters because each one is known to the Lord. Not 'many,' not 'some,' but two hundred and seventy-six. God keeps count when the sea roars and night closes in.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: After eating, they lightened the ship by throwing wheat into the sea—more cargo lost. But now the crew had strength to work. Sometimes you have to spend what you've saved to survive what's coming.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Daylight came at last. They saw a bay with a beach they didn't recognize—but it offered hope. They made a choice: steer for land. Sometimes salvation looks like a place you've never been.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Anchors cast off, rudder ropes freed, the foresail hoisted. The crew moved from despair to purpose. Every hand had work. In the moment of action, fear grows small and skill comes to the front.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Where two seas met, the vessel ran aground. The bow stuck fast, the stern began to break. The ship died, but the appointed island held them—not by gentleness, but by its solid, immovable presence.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The soldiers' counsel was to kill the prisoners—so none could escape and make the guards look bad. Even in disaster, the law was hard. But justice and mercy were about to clash.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The centurion Julius, wanting to save Paul, stopped the slaughter. He stayed the sword. Fourteen days in the pit had changed him—he saw Paul's God at work and could not kill him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Looking back on how the Lord's faithfulness moves through terrified people—a centurion becomes a protector, a ship is lost but every soul is saved, a prisoner's faith reshapes everyone around him. Today, readers hear an echo: when one person trusts Jesus wholly, whole households of fear find their way to shore.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
